title: What mystery did the original "clue" solve? | MYTHOLOGY WORDS

entries.note: Per the Oxford folklore dictionary, sacred stories about divine beings tied to religion, distinguished from [[see:legend]] and [[see:folk tale]].
Contrasted with [[see:myth]]; Rob associates legends with heroes, and a divine actor in a trivial story makes a religious legend.
What a [[see:myth]] becomes once its characters are no longer seen as gods but as heroes, giants or fairies.
Some indigenous storytellers feel the label is dismissive, treating their stories as less significant than myths.
From [[from:Tantalus]], cursed to stand in water beneath fruit that always recede beyond his reach.
Greek figure who fed his son [[see:Pelops]] to the gods and was punished in the underworld, giving [[gave:tantalize]].
Son of [[see:Tantalus]], served to the gods by his father.
From the nymph Echo, cursed by [[see:Hera]] to repeat others' words; spurned by [[see:Narcissus (myth)]], she wasted away until only her voice remained.
Unhealthy self-interest, from [[from:Narcissus (myth)]]; the Greek root means numbness or stupor, linking it to [[same-root:narcotic]].
Goddess who cursed [[see:echo]] over suspicions about [[see:Zeus]]'s affairs with nymphs.
Supposedly used Echo to distract [[see:Hera]] while he chased other nymphs.
Beautiful youth in love with his own reflection who rejected Echo and faded away, giving [[gave:narcissism]] and the flower [[gave:narcissus]].
Flowers said by Ovid to grow where [[from:Narcissus (myth)]] died, now called narcissi or [[see:daffodil]]s.
Another name for the [[see:narcissus]] flower.
Shares the Greek root meaning numbness with [[same-root:narcissism]].
From the Greek sleep god [[from:Hypnos]].
Greek god of sleep who gave [[gave:hypnosis]].
God of dreams, his name from Greek for shape as the shaper of dreams; source of [[gave:morphine]].
Named after [[from:Morpheus]], god of dreams.
Shaping something into human form, from the same Greek word for shape as [[same-root:Morpheus]].
Its morphing comes from the same root as [[same-root:Morpheus]] and [[same-root:morphine]].
From the goddess [[from:Aphrodite]].
Goddess behind [[gave:aphrodisiac]] and part of [[gave:hermaphrodite]].
A falling-out-of-use word combining [[from:Hermes]] and [[from:Aphrodite]], named after their son [[from:Hermaphroditus]].
God of science and art, part of [[gave:hermaphrodite]] and source of [[gave:hermetic]].
Son of [[see:Hermes]] and [[see:Aphrodite]], after whom [[gave:hermaphrodite]] is named.
An old word for hermaphroditism, comparable to [[equivalent:hermaphrodite]], that Rob was startled to hear translated.
From [[from:Hermes]]; first about occult science and alchemy, now airtight, as in hermetically sealed, from an airtight tube credited to [[see:Hermes Trismegistus]].
Egyptian god linked with [[see:Hermes]] and alchemy, behind the story of [[see:hermetic]].
Called 'thrice blessed Hermes', said to have invented an airtight glass tube, explaining [[see:hermetic]] sealing.
From [[from:Eros]]; means related to love, not necessarily sexual.
The Greek counterpart of [[see:Cupid]], source of [[gave:erotic]].
Roman counterpart of [[see:Eros]].
Previously discussed; means what is desired, sharing roots with [[same-root:venery]], [[same-root:venerate]], [[same-root:win]] and [[same-root:wish]].
Shares a root with [[same-root:Venus]].
Shares a root with [[same-root:Venus]].
Shares a root with [[same-root:Venus]].
From the same Proto-Indo-European root as [[same-root:Venus]].
From the same Proto-Indo-European root as [[same-root:Venus]].
Discussed in an earlier episode.
From a Greek word meaning to forget, via [[from:Lethe]], the river of Hades the dead drank from to forget their lives.
River of Hades whose waters made the dead forget, behind [[gave:lethargic]].
From Mentor, [[see:Telemachus]]'s mentor in the Odyssey; related to [[same-root:mental]] and [[same-root:mantis]], and distantly to [[same-root:muse]].
Character in the Odyssey whose adviser gave us [[see:mentor]].
Shares a root with [[same-root:mentor]].
Shares a root with [[same-root:mentor]].
The Muses were daughters of Zeus and protectors of the arts, now a source of inspiration; distantly related to [[same-root:mentor]].
From the same root as [[same-root:muse]].
From the same root as [[same-root:muse]].
Literally a temple to the Muses; see [[from:muse]].
Athenian who slew the [[see:Minotaur]] and escaped the [[see:labyrinth]] using a [[see:clue]], then abandoned [[see:Ariadne]].
Half-bull, half-man monster living in the [[see:labyrinth]] at Knossos.
Simply Greek for maze; already figurative in ancient Greece, meaning confusing arguments.
Old word for a ball of twine, like the one [[see:Ariadne]] gave [[see:Theseus]] to find his way out of the [[see:labyrinth]].
Daughter of [[see:Minos]] who gave Theseus the ball of twine, a [[see:clue]], then was dumped on an island.
King whose daughter [[see:Ariadne]] helped Theseus.
Named after [[from:Aegeus]], who threw himself into it on seeing Theseus's sail still black.
Theseus's father, who drowned himself in despair, giving the [[gave:Aegean Sea]] its name.
Greek monster whose name is now the genus name for jellyfish, their tendrils resembling her snaky hair; compare French [[same-root:méduse]].
French for [[equivalent:jellyfish]], which led Rob's wife to call a jellyfish a medusa in English.
The hosts find it a worse name than [[see:Medusa]], since the creature is not a fish.
Swedish biologist who standardised scientific naming and paired [[see:flora]] with [[see:fauna]].
From Flora, Roman goddess of flowers celebrated at [[see:Floralia]]; paired with [[see:fauna]] by [[see:Carl Linnaeus]].
Applied to animal life by [[see:Carl Linnaeus]]; from Fauna, a Roman fertility goddess linked to [[see:Faunus]].
Festival of the goddess Flora, behind [[see:flora]].
Roman forest god connected to the goddess behind [[see:fauna]]; his Greek counterpart is [[see:Pan]].
Startling night noises in the forest were blamed on [[from:Pan]]; first an adjective, as in panic terrors, like [[see:manic]].
Greek forest god who gave [[gave:panic]].
Compared to the original adjectival use of [[see:panic]].
Literally thunder lizard, inspired by [[from:Brontes]], one of the three [[see:Cyclopes]].
One of the [[see:Cyclopes]] who made Zeus's thunderbolt; inspired [[gave:brontosaurus]].
Three brothers, [[see:Brontes]], [[see:Steropes]] and [[see:Arges]], who made Zeus's thunderbolt.
Rob suggests it comes from the Titans, wondering whether the [[see:Cyclopes]] were Titans.
One of the [[see:Cyclopes]], named from the word for lightning.
One of the [[see:Cyclopes]], named from argos, shining or bright, also seen in the [[same-root:Argo]].
Shares the root meaning shining or bright with [[same-root:Arges]].
From Nemesis, goddess of retribution; the Greek means distribution of what is due, related to [[same-root:numerous]].
Related to [[same-root:nemesis]] through the idea of allocating.
An example of a month named after a Roman god, [[from:Janus]].
The two-faced god, discussed in an earlier episode.
Relating to war or the military, from [[from:Mars]], god of war.
Roman war god, equated with [[see:Ares]] and also the red planet; source of [[gave:martial]].
Greek war god corresponding to [[see:Mars]].
From astrology: born under the influence of the planet [[from:Jupiter]], associated with happiness, rather than the god himself.
Planet associated in astrology with joy, behind [[gave:jovial]]; the god himself isn't associated with happiness.
Means plentiful; corresponds to [[see:Copia]], Roman personification of abundance, and relates to [[same-root:cornucopia]].
Roman personification of plenty corresponding to [[see:copious]].
The horn of plenty, related to [[same-root:copious]].
From [[from:Ceres]], goddess of agriculture and grain.
Goddess of agriculture and grain behind [[gave:cereal]].
Related to [[from:Bacchus]]; came up recently over an Olympics opening ceremony.
Roman god behind [[gave:bacchanal]].
From [[from:Moneta]], a title of [[see:Juno]], whose temple stood on the hill where money was coined and precious metals stored.
Title of [[see:Juno]] meaning to advise, warn or admonish; source of [[gave:money]].
Roman goddess titled [[see:Moneta]], whose temple gave [[see:money]] its name.
From Latin [[from:fascinare]], to bewitch; once witches' power to enthral, positive since the 1800s; likely related to [[from?:fascinum]].
The divine phallus symbolising the god [[see:Fascinus]]; Roman penis effigies, some winged, invoked his protection; probably behind [[gave?:fascinate]].
Roman god symbolised by the [[see:fascinum]].
Named after the Anglo-Saxon god [[from:Tiw]], related to Norse [[see:Tyr]], a war god like Mars; compare [[equivalent:dies Martis]] and [[equivalent:mardi]].
Woden's day, after [[from:Woden]], the Anglo-Saxon equivalent of [[see:Odin]].
The only day named after a Norse god; Old English 'thunder day', with the modern form influenced by [[from:Thor]].
Named after [[from:Frigg]], not [[unrelated:Freya]], who is a different goddess.
Norse thunder god whose name influenced [[see:Thursday]].
A popular word of our times, now tacked onto anything to mean the background universe of a fictional story; also the podcast [[see:Lore (podcast)]].
A podcast about dark historical tales that Jess recommends.
Anglo-Saxon god behind [[gave:Tuesday]], related to Norse [[see:Tyr]].
Norse war god similar to [[see:Tiw]], connected to Mars.
Day of Mars, a counterpart of [[equivalent:Tuesday]] (called Greek by the hosts); source of French [[gave:mardi]].
French for [[equivalent:Tuesday]], the day of Mars.
Anglo-Saxon equivalent of [[see:Odin]], behind [[gave:Wednesday]].
Norse chief god, equivalent to [[see:Woden]].
Goddess after whom [[gave:Friday]] is named.
A different goddess from [[see:Frigg]], often wrongly thought to be behind [[see:Friday]].
The only other English word from Germanic gods Rob found: the name of [[from:Hel]], Norse goddess of the underworld.
Norse goddess of the underworld, spelled with one L, whose name gave [[gave:hell]].
Coined by [[see:Horace Walpole]] in the 1700s from [[from:The Three Princes of Serendip]], about princes making unsought discoveries.
Coined [[see:serendipity]] in the 1700s.
Persian fairy tale, in an English version, about princes making unsought discoveries; inspired [[gave:serendipity]].
Old Persian name for Sri Lanka, from a Sanskrit term meaning dwelling place of lion's island.
From Sanskrit for descent: a god's physical form on earth, now a person's representation in games, virtual worlds or account icons.
Film presumably named for transferring consciousness into blue bodies; Jess dislikes it, and Rob jokes the franchise is a [[see:juggernaut]].
Series Jess recommends, unlike the [[see:Avatar (film)]] films.
From Sanskrit [[from:Jagannath]], 'lord of all worlds', a title of [[see:Krishna]] whose huge cart-borne statue people supposedly threw themselves under.
Hindu god whose title gave [[gave:juggernaut]].
X-Men character who can burst through almost anything, named from [[from:juggernaut]].
